content.p: In the Van Diemen's Land of the 1820s there were two kinds of bushranger in the public mind. One was Matthew Brady, the polite robber whom women wrote love letters to. The other was Thomas Jeffries, a convict who flogged his fellow prisoners for a living, walked out of a Launceston watch house with a gun in December 1825, and spent about six weeks at large. The colonial press called him a monster. By the end of January 1826 the newspapers were reporting that he had confessed to killing a companion and living on the body for days, and that he had been present when a five-month-old infant was killed in front of its mother.

He was tried in Hobart, sentenced to death and hanged on 4 May 1826, on the same gallows day as Brady. Almost everything known about him comes from convict registers, a handful of colonial newspaper reports and the books written about the bushrangers decades later. These disagree on small matters and a few large ones, and the sections below say where.

The colonial registers give Thomas Jeffries's trade as painter. A police notice issued in Hobart in March 1825 gives his birthplace as Bristol, his age as 35, his height as 5 feet 9 and a quarter inches, and lists tattoos on his left arm, among them hearts and darts and flower pots. The notice says he had been tried at Nottingham in July 1817 and sentenced to life. The biography compiled by the Australian National University's People Australia project gives a different date, 29 July 1819, for a Nottingham conviction for burglary, and says he reached Sydney on the Prince Regent in January 1820. Convict Records, which reproduces the colonial registers, shows 1817 in some entries and 1819 in others, and in one a Middlesex trial. The disagreement is in the records themselves.

He was sent on to Van Diemen's Land aboard the Haweis. People Australia puts his arrival in January 1822, while the Gristly History blog says October 1823. James Bonwick, whose book on the colony's bushrangers was written well after the events, offered a quite different origin: a "Scotch seaman" who had been jailed in Edinburgh and had traded his sentence for a job as hangman. The registers give no support to that account, and it should be treated as folklore.

What the registers do show is a man who was repeatedly in trouble even before he took to the bush. In 1824 he was an overseer in the jail gang and was punished for threatening to stab the chief constable, George Lawson; the sentence was twelve months at Macquarie Harbour, though People Australia says he was kept instead on the public works at George Town. On 1 February 1825 he absconded from George Town and received 50 lashes. In April 1825 he was made flagellator at Launceston gaol, a post that put him in charge of whipping other convicts. People Australia's summary of the same conduct record has him fined 10 shillings on 3 August for being drunk and disorderly (Convict Records' transcription reads 20 shillings), fined two pounds on 25 August for falsely imprisoning and assaulting a Mrs Elizabeth Jessop, and fined a pound in October for taking a female prisoner out of the watch house.

The Gristly History blog adds that Jeffries was an officially sanctioned flogger who also sexually assaulted several women. That claim is the blog's own, and none of the registers quoted elsewhere mentions it. Bonwick said a drunken prisoner's feet were burned among hot ashes while Jeffries was keeper of the watch house, and that its discovery drove him into the bush. The People Australia entry does not mention that incident either.

On 14 December 1825, according to People Australia, Jeffries escaped from Launceston with three prisoners, Edward Russell, John Perry and James Hopkins. Russell's convict file records him as absconding on 15 December. The Hobart Town Gazette of 17 December reported that Jeffries had left the watch house with the three men and was carrying a gun. The Colonial Times, the day before, had noted that he was both flagellator and keeper of the watch house.

The men were not hardened veterans. Perry was a 19-year-old bricklayer from Battersea, transported for life for housebreaking, who had already been sentenced to the Macquarie Harbour penal station once for absconding. Russell was a 19-year-old painter and glazier who had reached the colony only that September, according to Convict Records. Hopkins, a stocking weaver from Gloucestershire, had been in the colony since December 1821. The gang quickly robbed a stock hut, and on 23 December the Colonial Times reported that they meant to join Brady's gang. A reward of 200 dollars for Jeffries and each of his men was advertised on 7 January 1826, and within a week the Colonial Times was arguing that it was too small.

The killing that fixed Jeffries in colonial memory happened at the home of a settler named Tibbs, about five miles from Launceston. The account that Gristly History reproduces from the colonial press says the men arrived about noon and tried to bind the occupants, Mr Tibbs, his wife of about two years, their child and a neighbouring settler's servant. When they resisted, the report says, the intruders shot two of them. One fell dead, and Tibbs was badly wounded but survived and raised the alarm. Mrs Tibbs was taken away and came back on Sunday afternoon in a state of distraction, and the infant had been killed.

George Boxall's History of the Australian Bushrangers tells it differently and in more detail. In his version the stockman was shot after refusing to go with the bushrangers, and Tibbs was shot when he rushed at Jeffries after the infant had been killed. Boxall says the mother was told to walk faster, said she could not with the baby in her arms, and had the child snatched from her and its brains dashed out against a sapling. The Gristly blog says the mother could not keep up with the fleeing gang and the child's head was smashed against a tree trunk. The burial register for 4 May 1826, quoted by Convict Records, says he killed a child of six months by dashing its brains out against a rock. The weapon is a rock in one source, a sapling in another, and a tree in a third; every source agrees on the infant's death.

The number of deaths varies widely. The Colonial Times of 13 January 1826 said the gang had killed three people including an infant. By 27 January it was arguing that Jeffries had committed six murders. People Australia counts seven killed during the few months on the run, while Bonwick says Jeffries himself confessed to five. Hobart Town Gazette reports summarised by People Australia say he shot Constable Bakie dead, with the spelling given in the paper, and that Perry later hanged in part for the deaths of Tibbs, the infant and the constable. Boxall describes another killing, of a settler named Baker who was shot at Georgetown while forced to carry a knapsack. No other page describes that incident.

The element that made Jeffries notorious beyond Launceston was cannibalism. People Australia's entry on Perry says the men, short of food, apparently cast lots to decide who should die, and that Russell lost. According to Jeffries' own confession after capture, he shot Russell in the head that night and the men lived on the flesh for four days. Boxall says Jeffries and Hopkins lived on it for five days and threw away about five pounds of Russell's flesh when they came to a sheep station, where they killed two sheep and told the shepherd they wanted a good feed. The Gristly blog says they were still carrying about five pounds of human flesh when they were seized. The Colonial Times of 27 January 1826 carried Jeffries' admission that Russell was killed and eaten because the gang was rather pressed for food.

People Australia reports that Hopkins separated from the others after a musket and supplies were stolen from Joseph Railton's house at Spring Plains near Evandale, and that he was the first of the gang to be caught, in January 1826.

The sources disagree about who took him. People Australia, citing the Colonial Times of 10 February 1826, says two convicts, William Parsons, who had a life sentence, and a man named Shean, captured him. Boxall credits John Batman, later one of the founders of Melbourne, who, Boxall says, brought Aboriginal trackers to the island, was engaged by the government to track and capture bushrangers, and had caught Hopkins and others. The People Australia entry on Hopkins gives the date differently from the press accounts: it says Jeffries and Perry were captured in February, while the Hobart Town Gazette of 28 January had already summarised his crimes and the Colonial Times a day earlier had printed his confession. The pages do not settle the date or the captors.

Gristly History says he surrendered without a fight and was ready to inform on his accomplices, and Bonwick agrees that he turned on his mates. Hobart Town Gazette's description of his arrival in Launceston, which the blog quotes, reads that the town was almost emptied of its inhabitants to meet him and that several attempts were made to take him from the cart, so that a stronger guard had to be sent for. Bonwick tells a more theatrical version in which the infant's mother broke through the soldiers and flew at him.

Brady was captured later and lodged in the same lock-up. Boxall says Brady was disgusted to find himself sharing the cart to Hobart with Jeffries and kept as far from him as he could. A report that the Brady gang planned to break into Launceston gaol and torture and shoot Jeffries is mentioned in both Boxall and Bonwick; neither says the gaol was attacked, and Boxall says the bushrangers entered the town and robbed a house but did not go to the gaol.

He was brought to Hobart in April 1826. The sources agree that he was sentenced at the same sessions as Perry, Hopkins and the remainder of Brady's gang. The Sydney Gazette of 17 May 1826 reported that he was found guilty of several murders, including that of the infant. People Australia says Hopkins, Jeffries and Perry were found guilty of stealing a gun from Joseph Railton's house, and Convict Records describes Perry as not guilty of murder but executed for the theft and for aiding and abetting a murder. A Hobart account reproduced by Convict Records says Chief Justice Pedder passed sentence on twelve prisoners on a Saturday, telling the men that the offences of Jeffries and Perry had been attended by circumstances so atrocious that he would not repeat them in court. It reports that Brady was composed, while Jeffries appeared much agitated.

The same account says Jeffries, who was held in a cell with the Protestants, became penitent. Hopkins was sentenced to death too, but on 12 May 1826 the sentence was commuted to transportation for life. A man of that name, probably the same one, was sent to Norfolk Island in February 1827 and absconded in 1833; his convict record simply says "Dead".

Executions were staged in two groups. On the first morning, according to the account, Jeffries, Perry, Thompson, Brady and Bryant were hanged, with the rest of the twelve to follow the next day. The Rev. Mr Bedford led Jeffries out first. He was described as firm and composed and prayed fervently. He was the first to climb onto the scaffold. Bedford told the crowd outside the gaol on his behalf that he attributed all his crimes to drunkenness, acknowledged the whole of the crimes charged, and urged the crowd to avoid the vice. The Hobart Town Gazette of 6 May recorded that Jeffries wished it known that he died justly.

The Executed Today and Hobart magazine pieces are about Brady, and their only mention of Jeffries is that Brady's one complaint about his own fate was having to share the scaffold with a cannibal, and the Hobart magazine adds the insult that Jeffries had informed on others. The Gristly blog's comment is that no one mourned him.

The artist Thomas Bock sketched Jeffries in the dock; the drawing, titled as showing him on trial for the murder of Mr Tibbs' infant, is held at the State Library of New South Wales (Dixson bequest). A photographer's note about the sketch warns against confusing him with a later Tasmanian prisoner of the same name, a locally born man photographed in Hobart gaol in October 1873 who the note suggests might have been the bushranger's grandson. That claim is speculation by the note's author, and the two men should not be mixed up.
